html:
The Darling River, Baaka or Barka in the Paakantyi language, is a river of the dry west of New South Wales in Australia. It runs about 1,470 kilometres from near Bourke to the Murray River at Wentworth and is the main stream of the largest river system in the country.

Its waterholes and lakes held fish, birds and plant foods. The Barkindji, whose name means "people of the river", held long stretches of it. Related groups such as the Bandjigali and the Barindji lived on the plains beside it, and the Kamilaroi on the rivers that feed it.

The explorer Charles Sturt reached it in 1829 and named it after the governor, Ralph Darling. From 1859 paddle steamers carried wool from its sheep stations down to South Australia. The Burke and Wills expedition set out north from its camp at Menindee in 1860.

Today much of its water is taken for irrigation upstream, and low flows have brought mass fish deaths at Menindee.
